> 「菩萨于法，应无所住，行于布施。所谓不住色布施，不住声香味触法布施。……若菩萨不住相布施，其福德不可思量。」

Section four gives the first instruction in the sutra, and it is not about meditation. It is about giving.

The instruction has a strange shape: 应无所住，行于布施 — *not abiding anywhere, practice giving.* Two clauses, and they pull in opposite directions. One says: act. The other says: do not take up a position.

## 住 is a verb about glue

住 is usually translated "abide" or "dwell", which sounds domestic and harmless. The book renders it as: to climb on, to stick to, to grasp, to leave a mark on.

The mind does this constantly and mostly invisibly. It sticks to the act (*I am the kind of person who gives*), to the object (*they needed me*), to the reward (*this will come back*), and to the feeling (*that felt good*). Each is a small adhesion, and each is what 住 means here.

## The six fields include the sixth one

住色, 住声香味触法 — form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and 法. The first five are external. The sixth is not: 法 in this list means the objects of mind — thoughts, images, opinions, the concepts you form about the giving while you are giving.

This is the part most readers skip. Not abiding in the five senses is comparatively easy to imagine. Not abiding in your own interpretation of your own generosity is the hard half, and it is where the section actually aims.

## 福德 is a functioning, not a deposit

福德 — merit, blessedness — is treated by popular Buddhism as a balance that accumulates and can be drawn against later. The sutra refuses this.

Merit is a conditional arising: causes meet conditions and a result appears. It functions; it is not a substance. There is no account, no ledger, no stored quantity that can be transferred or compared.

Which is why the next move is an image of measurement being broken. East, South, West, North, the four intermediate directions, above and below — the ten directions of space. Can they be measured? No. So it is with the merit of giving without abiding.

## 不可思量 has a trapdoor

The trapdoor is obvious once stated and almost always walked through anyway: if you give without abiding *in order to* obtain immeasurable merit, you have just abided — in immeasurable merit.

The sutra knows this. It does not offer the reward as motivation; it offers the image to dismantle the measuring mind. The moment the measuring stops, the comparison has nothing to stand on. That is the whole of the "immeasurable".

## What the section does not say

It does not say giving is cold. The book is explicit: non-abiding is not indifference. Indifference is a lack of compassion. Abiding is compassion with a grip attached. They are different failures, and the sutra is treating only the second.

It also does not say that only money counts. 布施 has three forms: goods, teaching, and fearlessness — the last being the giving of safety to someone who is afraid. Most people have more of the third to give than of the first, and give it less often.

## The test

Give something today — money, time, a piece of knowledge, or simply your attention to someone who is frightened. Something real, small enough that you will actually do it.

Then, an hour later, check what you are still holding. Are you holding the amount? The gratitude, or its absence? The image of yourself doing it?

Whatever you are still holding is the 住. The giving was fine. That is the part to look at.
